newsitem.title: FRANCE: French right starts polls drive with May Day parade.
newsitem.headline: French right starts polls drive with May Day parade.

text.p: French far-right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen and his National Front launched their drive for a foothold in parliament on Thursday with a May Day parade through the heart of the capital.

Le Pen's traditional May Day festival, honouring French mediaeval hero Joan of Arc who drove the English out of France, was broadened this year to carry Front hopes of winning seats in the National Assembly, where it currently has none.
Some 5,000 party loyalists turned out for the demonstration in bright sunshine as across the city leftist trade unions planned a labour march later in the day.

The Front, which wants to ship immigrants home and give a constitutional preference to "native-born French" in jobs and social benefits, has set a goal of 20 seats in parliamentary elections called for May 25 and June 1, enough to form a parliamentary group.
Pollsters predicted it could win at most a few seats, although voter surveys show it gathering rather more than the 15 percent Le Pen won in his 1995 presidential campaign.

Even if the Front fails to win seats, it could play a key role in some 200 of France's 577 constituencies by splitting the vote between candidates of the ruling centre-right and the leftist opposition.
In a worst case scenario for the centre-right, the Front could shove the left into power.

Le Pen, who announced on the eve of the parade that he would not himself run in the election, has targeted the centre-right, saying the Front's priority was to "zap" it from power even if it meant a victory for the left.
A Le Pen supporter, an elderly woman who would not give her name, said he had made "just the right move" in deciding not to run.
"He wants (President Jacques) Chirac to resign should he fail to win a majority, and Mr Le Pen wants to be available to launch his presidential campaign immediately," she said.
Police were much in evidence in the side-streets though the atmosphere was relaxed. Beefing up security were dozens of Le Pen's own burly guards, dressed in grey slacks and blazers.
Most in the parade were well-dressed, sporting suits and ties or dresses. But a number of skinheads in leather and heavy boots marched among the National Front Youth movement.

Marchers chanted "Le Pen for President" and "Neither right nor left" -- a slogan borrowed from France's World War Two Nazi occupation days -- as they marched past the golden statue of Joan of Arc on horseback on the rue de Rivoli facing the Tuileries gardens.
